$comment: What each surface is made of, for the reflections and the specular response.
The usual trick for an old game -- match texture names like snow* or metal* -- cannot work here.
I.G.I.'s textures are NUMBERED: level 1 draws 203_04_1, 216_01_1_argb8888, 219_02_1 and a hundred
more like them, and no rule over those strings knows which one is glass.
So there are two ways to name a surface below.
*suffix        matches any texture ending that way. The one piece of meaning the names carry is
_argb8888, which marks the textures the packs store with an alpha channel -- in
this game the glass, the wire fences and the foliage.
exact_name     matches that one texture. Laborious, and the only honest way to say that a
particular numbered texture is polished metal: someone has to look at it.
An exact name beats a suffix rule. Roughness runs 0 (a mirror) to 1 (chalk); metallic is very
nearly always 0 or 1, because a surface is either a conductor or it is not.
Concrete, dirt, snow, painted metal -- the overwhelming majority of the game.
0.6, and it was 0.8. Nothing else in the renderer moves a surface's roughness DOWN: the derived
map multiplies around this figure and the floor-gloss term only touches up-facing surfaces, so
whatever stands here is the floor for every wall in the game. At 0.8 that floor was already past
the point where a GGX lobe is a hemisphere -- every surface answered light identically, the
derived roughness map had nowhere to move, the screen-space reflections rejected every pixel
(r_ssr_max_roughness is far below it), and the specular anti-aliasing saturated without doing
anything. 0.6 is still matte for a wall and leaves headroom in both directions, which is what
makes the rest of the material pipeline able to say anything at all.

$metal: WHAT IS MADE OF METAL, and why it is here rather than in a texture channel.
The detail map's alpha used to carry metallic, and carried zero in every texel ever written,
because nothing that derives a map from a diffuse texture can possibly know: no photograph of a
surface distinguishes painted steel from grey paint, since the difference is in how each answers
light and not in what colour it is. Guessing from the picture puts a mirror finish on half the
level. So it is authored, here, by someone who looked -- and metal in I.G.I. is per MATERIAL
anyway rather than per texel: a fuel tank is steel over the whole of it and a wall is steel over
none of it.
Binary, per Filament's guidance and common physically based practice: a surface is a conductor or it is
not, and the values in between only exist for a texture that mixes the two. Roughness 0.45 is
worn industrial steel -- these are not polished, and none of them were clean in 1998 either.
SIXTY-EIGHT TEXTURES, OUT OF 1152. This is a starting set, not a finished survey: it is the
textures that are unmistakably bare metal when looked at FULL SIZE, drawn from a contact sheet
of the 506 whose colour is near-neutral with real tonal variation in it. Full size matters: at
thumbnail size a weathered concrete panel and corrugated steel siding are the same picture, and
seven entries that survived the thumbnail pass were struck after the larger one -- one of them a
concrete wall that this turned into 42% of a test viewpoint. Everything not named here stays a
dielectric, which is the safe way to be wrong -- a metal drawn as a dielectric looks like a
duller version of itself, where a dielectric drawn as metal loses its diffuse colour entirely
and reads as coloured chrome. Adding to this list is a texture at a time and needs no code.
$metal-plant: Plant and machinery: pipes and their bores, ducting, perforated mesh, equipment racks and the
machined faces of the interiors. The 1xx family is this game's industrial kit and holds most of
$metal-fittings: Fittings: shutter housings, handrails, bore-facing ends, panel edges. Named one at a time rather
than by family, because 2xx and 3xx are overwhelmingly painted concrete and a family rule there
would put a chrome finish on half a level.
$metal-exterior: Exterior metal: corrugated siding, louvred vents, roller shutters, bolted flanges, barred gates.
The 4xx-6xx families are buildings, and these are the parts of them that are not masonry.

$comment: The cut-out surfaces: anything the packs store with an alpha channel. Sixty-eight textures in
the whole game, and they were ALL given roughness 0.08 here on the reading that this suffix
marks glass.
It does not. Surveyed: the sixty-eight are window panes, wire fences, railings, cables, road
signs, ladders, scaffolding, foliage -- and smoke sprites. Ranked by how much alpha perimeter
each carries per unit of solid area, they run from 0.012 (a few large flat panes, glass-like)
to 0.79 (wire and leaves), with the median at 0.149. Perhaps ten of them are glass.
The blanket roughness is therefore REMOVED and these take the default. It was a defensible
compromise while the only consequence was a faint Fresnel on the screen-space reflections; it
stopped being one when the deferred pass gained a real specular lobe, because near-mirror
roughness on a bush puts a sharp highlight on every leaf, and on a smoke sprite it is worse.
Glass wants naming individually, which means somebody looking at ten textures rather than
trusting a suffix. The ranking above is the starting list, not the answer -- a large flat
alpha region is just as likely to be a road sign or a door.
$occlusion: Left out of the ambient occlusion, as occluder and as receiver. These are the cut-out
surfaces -- wire fences, foliage, glass -- and a depth buffer cannot describe them: it says
where a surface starts and never where it ends, so the horizon search treats a wire as a
solid slab reaching to infinity and darkens everything behind it.

$glass: THE TEN THAT REALLY ARE GLASS, named individually as the note above asks for.
Found by a metric the perimeter ranking could not supply. Perimeter per unit of solid area
finds surfaces with a lot of CUT-OUT edge, which is the right question for wire and foliage and
the wrong one for glazing: the windows it put at the top of the list -- 425_02_1, 425_03_1,
346_01_1, 405_01_1, 454_02_1 -- are frames around a hole. Their panes are FULLY transparent,
there is no glass in the texture at all, and the only pixels a material would reach are the
painted frame. Giving those a mirror finish would polish the window surround and nothing else.
Glass is where alpha is PARTIAL: a surface seen through but not completely. Ranking the
sixty-nine by the fraction of texels at intermediate alpha separates the two cleanly -- framed
panes and plain sheets at the top, then smoke, then the cut-outs, which carry almost no
intermediate alpha because a cut-out is a binary stencil.
Seven are architectural glazing and each is majority pane by area, so the frame in the same
texture is the minority the per-texture material has to lose. Three are plain translucent
sheets with no structure at all, which is what a pane fill looks like at 8x8.
DELIBERATELY LEFT OUT, all of them translucent and none of them glass: 433_01_1 (water),
map display), 301_02_1 (a sign), 344_01_1 (a flat red tint that may be a lamp lens or may be
an additive glow -- it is 16x16 and there is no way to tell from the texture), 700_28_1 (a
64x8 alpha gradient, which reads as a soft edge rather than a pane) and 009_09_1.
castsOcclusion is repeated on every entry and that is not redundant: an exact name BEATS the
suffix rule rather than extending it, and an entry that omits the flag takes the file default,
which is true. Leaving it off would have each of these start blocking the ambient occlusion and
the gather rays -- so naming a pane as glass would stop light passing through it.
0.08 is the figure the suffix rule used to carry, and it is well under r_ssr_max_roughness
(0.5 on enhanced and above, 0.22 on vanilla), so these march a screen ray on every preset.
glass:true is what actually puts a pane on screen, and without it the roughness above reached
only the FRAME. Deferred shading cannot blend, so the geometry pass resolves partial alpha into
keep-or-discard: the dithered coverage path needs an alpha GRADIENT, which a cut-out edge has and
a flat pane does not, so a pane at alpha 72 took the hard alpha<0.5 cut and every texel of it was
thrown away. That left the opaque frame in the same texture as the only part of these seven that
survived -- so the 0.08 landed on the glazing bars and made them read as polished metal, while
the glass itself was not transparent but absent. The flag holds these out of the G-buffer and
draws them in the forward translucency subpass instead, which is the one place a pane can both
show the room behind it and carry a reflection of its own.
$glass-windows: Framed panes: a mullioned window with translucent glass between the bars.
$glass-panes: Plain sheets: uniform partial alpha, no structure. 716_01_1 is 8x8 and every texel of it is
alpha 72, which is a pane fill and cannot be anything else.
